extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, natural philosophers, and experimental scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and illustrates the canonical methods for inductive causal inference (Method of Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, etc.) with worked examples and practical requirements for experimental design and corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple instances share the same consequent, identify what common antecedent they all share; that shared antecedent is a candidate for the proximate cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples where diverse antecedents otherwise differ but the same antecedent (e.g., metallic compounds combining with tissues) is present in all poisonous cases. Note limitation: the Method of Agreement alone cannot determine causation (it establishes invariable co-existence but not which is cause/effect or whether both result from something else).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a positive instance (effect present) and a negative instance (effect absent) that agree in all circumstances except one; the differing circumstance is inferred to be the cause (or part of it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a 'positive' and 'negative' instance differing in only a single circumstance. Examples: using antidotes (hydrated peroxide of iron counteracting arsenious acid) and the absence of poisoning when the poison is converted into an insoluble compound. Caveat: perfect single-difference is often unattainable because a single substance has many properties; be cautious about attributing causation without further corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference / Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict Method of Difference is unattainable, combine Agreement and Difference across many instances: find many antidotes or counterinstances that all share a single relevant property while differing otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many different substances act as antidotes and all agree in one property (e.g., forming insoluble compounds with the poison) while not agreeing in other properties, this strongly supports that property being the proximate cause. This method can approach the rigor of Method of Difference even if not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If varying the magnitude of one antecedent is accompanied by systematic variation in the consequent, infer a causal (or contributing) relation between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when antecedent and consequent vary in degree (a 'scale of intensity'). Examples: Leyden jar capacity and charge limits tied to neighboring body's capacity; deposition of dew correlates with power to resist conduction or to radiate heat. Useful when the quality in question cannot be excluded entirely because it is present in degrees rather than as a binary property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise Definition and Delimitation of Phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Before investigating causes, define exactly what the phenomenon is and what is excluded (e.g., distinguish dew from rain, fog moisture, or visible wet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a preliminary operation: limit the application of the term to the spontaneous appearance of moisture on substances exposed in the open air when no rain or visible wet is falling. Proper definition clarifies the facts to be explained and ensures relevant comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by Deductive Reasoning (Use of Known Laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Support an inductive hypothesis by deducing the observed consequent from well-established general laws (e.g., laws of heat and vapor tension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show deductively that cooling a surface lowers the air layer temperature and thus causes condensation because air holds less vapor at lower temperature. Deduction can both prove causation and account for exceptions (e.g., dry air prevents dew even if surface is cooled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Experimentation as a Test of Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduce the effect by manipulating the putative cause under controlled conditions (e.g., cool a surface until dew forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct experiments provide strong evidence: produce the antecedent (cooling) and observe the consequent (dew) at a determinable threshold. Even small-scale experiments, repeated and well-controlled, can validate causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural or 'Field' Experiments as Demonstrations of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Use naturally occurring changes that introduce a single definite new circumstance to test causal hypotheses (e.g., clouds withdrawing and the subsequent rapid deposition of dew).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such natural experiments can satisfy Method of Difference requisites when nature effects the change sharply and rapidly so that other factors remain essentially constant, thereby corroborating causal inferences made in the laboratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control via Paired or Within-Subject Comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two closely matched cases (e.g., opposite limbs of the same animal) where one differs in the antecedent of interest to infer causal effects while minimizing confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: paralyzed muscle versus corresponding healthy muscle on the opposite side of the same animal—assumed to differ only in paralysis. This within-subject control approximates the ideal single-difference requirement and strengthens causal attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication Across Subjects to Exclude Accidental Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat experiments across multiple subjects and instances to exclude the possibility that observed differences are due to accidental or idiosyncratic conditions of a single case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single paired experiment; replicate sufficiently often in different animals (or systems) so that accidental pathological or situational differences cannot account for the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Reversals and Temporal Variation as Causal Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that changing the antecedent leads to a corresponding change (or reversal) in the consequent over time, thereby strengthening the causal link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after paralysis-induced increased irritability (and later loss of irritability with prolonged rest), the cadaveric rigidity and putrefaction timings reverse correspondingly. Observing the effect reverse when the antecedent reverses provides strong causal evidence (A B C, a b c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination and Examination of Apparent Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate counterexamples that at first seem to disconfirm the hypothesis and explain them (e.g., why nitrate of silver is caustic externally but harmless when ingested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent exceptions may lead to discovery of intervening factors (stomach chloride converting nitrate to insoluble chloride of silver). Study exceptions to refine the causal account and identify additional necessary or sufficient conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that Causes and Effects Co-vary and Cease Together
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that the presence/quantity of the cause is tied to the presence/quantity of the effect and that both arise and dissipate together (e.g., opposite electricities are produced and cease together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple methods (Agreement, Concomitant Variations, Difference) to demonstrate that the possibility and amount of one are 'an impassable limit' to the other. Corroborate with experiments (e.g., Leyden jar behavior, Faraday's wire experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of Limitations: Correlation ≠ Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some methods (notably Method of Agreement) establish invariable co-existence but do not by themselves establish cause-effect direction or rule out a common cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always seek additional corroboration (Difference, Concomitant Variations, Deduction, direct experiment). Be explicit about the inferential gap when only agreement-type evidence is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Multiple Independent Lines of Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine several methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Deduction, experiment, natural experiment) to achieve high confidence in causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dew theory example: agreement (cold surfaces), concomitant variations (radiation/conduction/texture), deduction (vapor laws), direct experiments (cooling surfaces), and natural experiments (clouds withdrawing) together provide a 'fullness of assurance' not attainable by any single method alone.
